title: The Dream of Ignorance
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Q: Why is it said that “all dharmas are illusions”?

inline.s: (Excerpted from
The True Nature of All Dharmas
Q: Why is it said that “all dharmas are illusions”?

A: Because all sentient beings are in the dream of ignorance, and all dharmas are affairs within the dream of ignorance. All the myriad things of the universe are illusions produced by a single stirring thought that loses the true nature. Yongjia’s Song of Realizing the Way says:
“In the dream the six realms are clearly present; after awakening all is empty and still, and the great thousand worlds are gone.”
(In the dream of ignorance the six paths of rebirth are clearly present; when the dream of ignorance is over, all is serene and still—the great thousand worlds are nowhere to be found.)
The Mahāyāna Ghanavyūha Sūtra says:
“Like forms in a dream
(form objects—the things that can be seen)
, seen only by deluded imagination; on waking they are no more
(gone upon waking)
In the dream of ignorance
one sees all manner of forms, such as men and women; at true awakening
(becoming a Buddha)
nothing at all is seen.”

[Samyak-sambodhi] True awakening—becoming a Buddha is called attaining true awakening. [On attaining true awakening nothing is seen] Sentient beings, within the serene and unborn nature, see only arising and ceasing; the Buddhas, within the manifest arising and ceasing, see only the unborn.
In the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment the World-Honored One reveals that sentient beings are in the dream of ignorance:

“What is ignorance? Good man! All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all manner of inversion, like a lost man who mistakes the four directions for one another. They falsely take the four great elements as their own body and the shadow of the six sense objects as their own mind. They are like a man with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In the sky there are truly no flowers; the sick man falsely grasps at them. Because of this false grasping, he not only is deluded about the nature of empty space, but also is confused about the place where the real flowers arise. From this false existence they turn through birth and death—this is called ignorance. Good man! This ignorance has no real substance;
like a man in a dream

, while dreaming it is not nothing, but upon waking nothing whatsoever is obtained. Like the many flowers in the sky that vanish into space, one cannot say there is a fixed place where they cease. Why? Because there is no place where they arise. All sentient beings, within the unborn, falsely see arising and ceasing; therefore they are said to turn through birth and death.”

[The four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has wetness, fire has warmth, and wind has movement. All tangible matter in the world possesses these four natures—solidity, wetness, warmth, and motion—and therefore they are called “great.” Here the four great elements refer to the body. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Always sustain this thought: this body of mine is a union of the four great elements. What is called hair and fur, nails and teeth, skin and flesh, sinews and bones, marrow and brain, and the dregs of the body all return to earth; saliva and phlegm, pus and blood, bodily fluids, spittle, sputum, tears, essence, urine, and excrement all return to water; warmth returns to fire; movement returns to wind. When the four great elements each depart, where will this false body be?”

[The shadow of the six sense objects] The various thoughts produced by the six sense organs in dependence on the six sense objects—and all such thoughts are unreal and without substance—hence they are called the shadows of the six sense objects: the fleeting reflections of the six objects.
The Sūtra of Divination for Good and Evil Karmic Retribution says:

“Among such sentient beings, when the dharmakāya has been strongly perfumed, the afflictions gradually thin; able to weary of the world and to seek the path of nirvāṇa, to take refuge in the One Reality and to cultivate the six pāramitās and all the factors of enlightenment—these are called bodhisattvas. Among such bodhisattvas, when the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas is fulfilled,
those who at last depart from the sleep of ignorance are in turn called Buddhas
It also says:
“With all meritorious practices fulfilled, one becomes a Buddha. That is to say, relying on the ultimate bodhisattva ground, one can remove all obstructions;
the dream of ignorance
is exhausted.”
The Sūtra on the Kingly Dharma Spoken by the Buddha to the Heavenly Prince of Victorious Light says:
“All dharmas have an empty nature and are subject to impermanence and destruction. It is as when a person,
in a dream at night,
sees fine gardens, mountains and rivers, throngs of people, thick forests and clear springs, halls and pavilions—all delightful—and upon waking
(waking up)
sees nothing at all.”
Master Hanshan says:

“The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddha—fundamentally undefiled, and without the marks of birth, death, coming, or going. Yet because of an initial unawareness they are confused about their original nature, and so it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, all sorts of deluded thoughts arise, various inversions follow, and various karmas are performed, falsely taking up the suffering of birth and death within the three realms. All of this is ignorance: not understanding one’s own mind, and turning along with deluded thought. Like a person in deep sleep who dreams evil dreams—all kinds of states, all kinds of terrors, suffering beyond endurance. And when he wakes, seeking the affairs of the dream, he cannot get them at all. Therefore sentient beings, fallen into
the dream of ignorance
, turn along with deluded, inverted thoughts, perform all kinds of karmas, and bring suffering upon themselves. With awakened eyes, how could these inverted states be obtained?”
(Dream Wandering Collection
Instructions to Dong Zhiguang)

[The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by beings who still have the two desires of sexuality and food; it extends from the six heavens of desire above, through humans and animals in the middle, down to hungry ghosts and the hells below. The realm of form is the world inhabited by beings who have no desire for sexuality or food but still have a form body; it includes the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas. The formless realm is the world inhabited by beings who no longer have a form body but abide with mind-consciousness in deep and subtle meditative concentration; it includes the four formless heavens (the Heaven of Boundless Space, the Heaven of Boundless Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothing Whatsoever, and the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception). These three realms are all the states in which ordinary beings revolve through birth and death; hence the Buddhist practitioner’s first aim is to depart from the three realms.
Master Hanshan says:
“The Buddha said:
all dharmas are like a dream and an illusion
. He also said: birth and death and nirvāṇa
are like last night’s dream
(Dream Wandering Collection
Reply to Prefect Yuan Cangru)
The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“These bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age who, cultivating this mind, attain accomplishment—for them there is nothing to cultivate here and nothing attained. Perfect enlightenment shines universally, and quiescent extinction is non-dual
(the true nature of all dharmas)
; within it are hundreds, thousands, myriads, kotis of asaṃkhyeyas of Buddha-worlds, countless as the sands of the Ganges, like flowers in the sky
(illusions)
, rising in confusion and ceasing in confusion. Not identical
(not dwelling in any dharma)
, not separate
(not abandoning any dharma)
, with no bondage and no liberation; then one knows that sentient beings were originally Buddhas, and that birth and death and nirvāṇa
are like last night’s dream

[Quiescent extinction, non-dual] Because there is nothing at all, it is called quiescent extinction, non-dual. [Within it] Within the true realm of perfect enlightenment, which is quiescent extinction, non-dual. [Asaṃkhyeya] Translated into Chinese it is “countless” (wuyangshu)—meaning so many that no number can count them. [Birth and death and nirvāṇa are like last night’s dream] Both birth and death and nirvāṇa are affairs within the dream of ignorance; now that the dream of ignorance is over, looking back at past events is like the dream of last night.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra
vol. 576 says:
“If sentient beings could truly and fully realize
that all dharmas are like illusions and magical creations

, they would already have attained supreme enlightenment; but because sentient beings, with regard to all dharmas, cannot fully comprehend that all are like illusions and magical creations, they turn through birth and death in the various destinies.”
The Sūtra of the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata of the Great Vaipulya says:
“All Tathāgatas, relying on this samādhi, accomplish measureless great awesome spiritual power, and even realize the emptiness of all dharmas
(all dharmas are illusions)

, and are able to display all manner of sovereign, effortless deeds in all Buddha-lands of the ten directions. It is as when a person dreams of all kinds of changing events; upon waking, what was seen is all gone. Ordinary beings are likewise: because of
the dream of ignorance

, they falsely conceive that dharmas have real substance. The Buddhas, being awakened, cling to nothing; therefore in all worlds of the ten directions, in a single thought they display measureless Buddha-deeds, sovereign and unobstructed, benefiting and perfecting all sentient beings, causing them all to awaken and enter the measureless, deep, and wondrous doors of liberation.”

All the sūtras and treatises above are saying this: sentient beings are deluded within the dream of ignorance and turn in inversion; while the Buddhas, with the dream of ignorance exhausted, are sovereign over dharmas, and throughout the worlds of the ten directions display all manner of Buddha-deeds to deliver sentient beings.
Master Hanshan’s Dream Wandering Collection
Reply to Prefect Yuan Cangru also says:
“In the bodhisattva’s practice, even before the seventh ground, none has yet broken
the dream of ignorance

. All along, teaching sentient beings and accomplishing Pure Lands are all Buddha-deeds within a dream. Therefore a bodhisattva of the eighth ground is like one who crosses a river in a dream, still without awareness; only upon reaching Buddhahood is he called greatly awakened. This is said plainly and recorded fully in the Flower Ornament Sūtra—clear and certain evidence.”

The dream of ignorance is a great dream, like a virtual world, in which a great many dreamers interact with one another and can even build and destroy the environment and its objects. Yet people find it hard to believe that “we are in the dream of ignorance, and all dharmas are illusions.” This is not strange: if you have never awakened, how would you know you are in a dream? And yet, throughout the ages, countless people who have awakened the mind and seen their nature have all confirmed that we are in the dream of ignorance. Master Yongjia’s Song of Realizing the Way says:
“In the dream the six realms are clearly present; after awakening all is empty and still, and the great thousand worlds are gone.”
Through our own practice we too can verify this—this is the reproducibility of science.
[Reference material] There is now a view in the scientific world that the universe is a virtual world with an extremely complex program. Its program follows two basic principles (game rules):

1. The principle of mind-directed guidance. The moment the mind of the player moves, the system of this virtual world activates for him; when the player’s mind is still and unmoved (not even a subtle thought is present), the system of this virtual world automatically shuts down for him. This is the meaning of “all dharmas are only mind”: when the mind arises, all dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all dharmas cease.

2. The principle of dynamic revision. According to what the player’s avatar does in the virtual world, the system ceaselessly and dynamically revises and corrects the data of his destiny, thereby determining his present state and his future. If one does good, destiny turns toward the good; conversely, if one does evil, destiny turns toward the evil. Destiny is always self-made and self-received—this is karmic retribution.
A dream—if you take it as real, you come under its thralldom. Master Taixu says:
The mind within the dream
, is the mind of ordinary beings;
the mind that knows it is dreaming within the dream
, is the mind of bodhisattvas;
the awakened
(waking from the dream)
mind
, is the mind of the Buddha.”
(Outline of Consciousness-Only Contemplation)
The Compendium of the Meanings of the Mahāyāna says:

“Buddha is a name established from virtue. The Buddha is awareness, and from this the designation is set. Awareness has two senses: first, awareness as vigilance—as when a man is aware of a thief; second, awareness as full awakening—as when a man wakes from sleep
(waking from sleep)

. The awareness of vigilance counteracts the affliction-obstacle; the harm of afflictions is like a thief, and only the sage is aware so as not to be harmed by it, and therefore it is called awareness. The Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: “As a man aware of a thief is such that the thief can do nothing against him, so is the Buddha.” The awareness of full awakening counteracts the knowledge-obstacle; the dim slumber of ignorance is like sleep, and when holy wisdom arises one suddenly and fully awakens,
like one who wakes from sleep
(waking from a dream)

, and therefore it is called awareness. Since one can awaken oneself and also awaken others, and the practice of awakening reaches its fulfillment, one is therefore called a Buddha. Saying “self-awakening” distinguishes it from ordinary beings; saying “awakening of others” shows it differs from the two vehicles; and the full perfection of the practice of awakening manifests its difference from bodhisattvas.”

[The affliction-obstacle] Because ordinary people do not know the emptiness of the self and cling to a self, and because of that self they give rise to greed, anger, ignorance, and other afflictions, thereby obstructing the manifestation of nirvāṇa—hence it is called an obstacle. [The knowledge-obstacle] This is the obstacle of the knowable. Because ordinary people do not know the emptiness of dharmas and cling to all dharmas, they produce various kinds of mistaken knowledge that obstruct the arising of bodhi—hence it is called an obstacle. A sūtra says: “If the attachment to dharmas is not removed, the knowledge-obstacle arises and obstructs bodhi.”
Therefore the practice must be carried out in two aspects: first, vigilance—the moment a thought arises, know it; second, full awakening—no longer clinging to characteristics.
Q: The great masters of old spoke of a “dream within a dream”—what does this mean?

A: “The dream of ignorance” is the first word “dream.” Self-nature is the dreamer within the dream of ignorance, and self-nature falsely clings to the physical body as its own body and to the shadows of the six sense objects as its own mind; hence there is birth and death (birth-and-death in sections) and the round of rebirth—this is the second word “dream,” dreaming the dream of rebirth within the dream of ignorance. The ancients called it “dreaming again within a dream.” Body and mind are the dreamers within the dream of rebirth. When afflictions are cut off entirely, one ends birth-and-death in sections and emerges from the dream of rebirth; when ignorance is cut off entirely, one ends birth-and-death in transformation and emerges from the dream of ignorance.

[Birth-and-death in sections] Among sentient beings in the three realms and six destinies, because of the karmic retribution produced by good and evil deeds, their lifespans all have limits and their bodies all have segments; hence their birth and death is called “birth-and-death in sections.” One who ends birth-and-death in sections is released from the round of rebirth and departs from the three realms. [Birth-and-death in transformation] The sages of the three vehicles, having already severed the delusions of views and thought and ended birth-and-death in sections, in the course of cultivation find deluded imaginings gradually extinguished and realized understanding gradually increased. This migration between confusion and awakening is different in each stage; moving from an earlier stage into a later one is just like passing through a death and rebirth, and its transformation is mysterious and inconceivable—hence it is called “birth-and-death in transformation.” One who ends birth-and-death in transformation perfectly realizes Buddhahood.
Q: How does one leave the dream of rebirth?
A:

To leave this dream of rebirth, this ceaseless turning of birth and death, one must accomplish it through practice. The conventional path is to cut off all afflictions so that at the moment of death one is in control; then one can end birth and death and leave the round of rebirth. Patriarch Huangbo says:
“When an ordinary person is about to die, he need only contemplate the five aggregates
(form, feeling, thought, formations, consciousness)

as empty, the four great elements as without self, the true mind as without characteristics, neither going nor coming—at birth the nature does not come, at death the nature does not go. Serenely still and fully still, the mind and its realm are one. If one can in this way directly and suddenly awaken, and not be bound by the three times, then one is a person who has transcended the world.”
(Essentials of the Transmission of Mind.) If one practices the Pure Land path, one need only at the moment of death sustain ten consecutive recitations (see
The Conditions for Rebirth
), and be moved by Amitabha Buddha to come and welcome one, and then leave the dream of rebirth and be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
